claims.text: The initial Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu elemental distribution is homogeneous.
Cooling rate controls local compositional fluctuations in the nanoparticles.
Cooling-rate-dependent compositional fluctuations mediate the formation of interfacial phases during premelting.
The interfacial phases alter the onset of melting.
The interfacial phases alter the melting pathway.
Slower cooling permits greater atomic diffusion.
Enhanced diffusion under slower cooling produces localized elemental segregation.
Localized elemental segregation produces interfacial phases or phase boundaries.
The interfacial phases stabilize regions of the nanoparticles against melting.
Faster cooling traps a homogeneous solid solution.
Slow-cooled particles will exhibit distinct intermediate microstructures with observable phase boundaries relative to conventionally cooled particles.
Slow-cooled particles will exhibit a detectable difference in melting onset or melting profile relative to conventionally cooled particles.
The proposed mechanism applies to nanoscale Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy particles with an initially homogeneous elemental distribution.
Within the proposed applicability regime, diffusion distances are comparable to particle dimensions.
The magnitude of the melting-onset shift and the structure of the interfacial phases may depend on particle size and the exact cooling profile.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as varying cooling rate during the transition from premelting to melting, whereas the mechanism and experiment imply that cooling first establishes segregation and that melting is then measured during subsequent heating. The timing and order of cooling versus melting are therefore inconsistent.
